name: Tremont House (the first)

documented_range.note: BOTH ENDS ARE ATTESTED, WHICH IS RARE HERE. Andreas, printed p. 635: 'In 1833, the first Tremont House, situated then on the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, was built by Alanson Sweet.' The end is dated to the day, twice in the same volume: 'was managing it at the time it burned, October 27, 1839' (p. 635) and, in the year-by-year narrative, 'October 27, the most disastrous fire occurred that had ever visited Chicago. It commenced on Lake Street, near Dearborn. The Tremont House and seventeen other buildings were burned.' chicagology_prefire021's 1874 Tribune letter agrees on the year - 'In the fall of 1839, the Tremont House was first consumed by fire.' THE FROM DATE IS A BOUND, NOT A DATE: no source gives a month in 1833, so 1833-01-01 is the earliest day the attested year permits. The scene date sits nearly two years inside the range under any reading of that month, so nothing in this record turns on it - unlike the Steamboat Hotel, where the same kind of bound is the whole risk.

position.symbolic_location: North-west corner of Lake Street and Dearborn Street (today West Lake Street at North Dearborn Street), fronting south onto Lake.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND AGREED BY TWO INDEPENDENT PERIOD TEXTS; THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas, p. 635: 'situated then on the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets'. The Chicago Tribune letter of 2 February 1874, transcribed on chicagology_prefire021: 'In 1833 there was built upon the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets an unpretending frame structure known as the Tremont House.' Chicago Illustrated of January 1866, on the same page, gives 'the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn streets' a third time. DO NOT USE THAT PAGE'S HEADER, which says 'SE corner of Lake and Dearborn Streets' - data/sources/chicagology_prefire021.json records that the header describes the LATER Tremonts (the 1850 brick house by Van Osdel) and contradicts every body text on its own page. Andreas confirms the move: the house begun in December 1839 was built 'on the corner where the present Tremont stands', which is a different corner from the one that burned. METHOD, the project's standard one: Lake Street and Dearborn Street both survive on their 1830 plat lines, and the modern West Lake Street / North Dearborn Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447772.72, N 4637283.04 (OSM node 27477597, fetched 2026-08-11 - the same node and the same figures data/structures/dole_warehouse_south.json used). The building's south face is set on the Lake Street frontage 12.2 m north of that centre and its east face on the Dearborn frontage 12.2 m west of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834; the stored coordinate is the polygon origin AFTER the 180 degree facade bearing, which under the renderer's convention (renderers/web/js/walker.js) puts it at the building's north-east corner. Currey has the 1830 Thompson plat laying streets 'uniformly 66 feet wide', which would move each offset 2.1 m; that discrepancy is already recorded in docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md section 5. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, which is the georeference's residual (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), not an additional guess. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Lake Street, which is an inference from the street and not a statement: no source says which way the house fronted, and the corner would equally admit a Dearborn Street front. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS NOW MODELLED: the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield was extended east and its box now runs local E -320..+1700 and N -400..+400 (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/heightfield.json), so this footprint sits on real terrain and the validator measures its contact rather than clamping at a box edge. It lands within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground_contact declaration. That is new as of this parcel: docs/LIBERTIES.md L40 - two thirds of the town standing on ground that had not been built - is already in that document's Resolved section, and this record is written on the far side of that resolution: no Lake Street building in this parcel needed a ground_contact declaration. EVIDENCE CORRECTION 2026-10-26: the 30 x 20 ft envelope is smaller than the earlier 50 x 30 ft reconstruction. Preserve both existing street-facing planes, east E 447760.52 and south N 4637295.24, rather than shrinking at a fixed northeast origin. At bearing 180, N_origin=N_south+6.096=4637301.336 and E_origin stays 447760.52. This is derived placement within the existing uncertain street control, not a new survey or a change to the street grid.

construction.note: FRAME IS DOCUMENTED THREE TIMES OVER; THE FRAMING SYSTEM IS NOT. Andreas, of the first Tremont and its 1840 successor together: 'Both of these structures were of wood and far different in style and cost of construction from the costly edifice which to-day ranks among Chicago's leading hotels.' The 1874 Tribune letter calls it 'an unpretending frame structure'; Chicago Illustrated of January 1866 calls it 'a wooden structure'. What none of them says is whether it was braced or balloon framed. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date - the same value and the same reasoning as data/structures/green_tree_tavern.json, built the same year. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail.

stories.note: Optional two-storey reading of Gale1902p51, in the town walk framed by arrival in1835. This is retrospective textual evidence, not a second picture. Gifford actually shows three storeys, which the primary reconstruction retains. No dated enlargement reconciles them.

gallery.note: NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY. False is what the archetype falls back to, not a finding, and the consequence is the one docs/LIBERTIES.md L19 records for the Green Tree and the Western: a plain front reads as the answer while a drawn shape at least announces itself as a choice. A stage house on the town's principal crossing is exactly the type that often carried a porch - and the 1874 letter's complaint that around this corner in early spring 'it was impossible to drive the stage, and the passengers had to walk some two blocks' says stages came here without saying what they drew up under.

sidewalk.note: A DOCUMENTED ABSENCE, AND ONE OF THE FEW THINGS ANYBODY WROTE DOWN ABOUT THIS BUILDING. Ira Couch, who took the house in 1834, 'found the house a mere shell, WITHOUT ANY SIDEWALK AROUND IT, and poorly furnished' - Chicago Tribune, 2 February 1874, transcribed on chicagology_prefire021. The same letter, under 'The Muddy Days': 'Around this corner, in early spring-time, it was impossible to drive the stage, and the passengers had to walk some two blocks; on account if the marshy state of the ground, the horses could not navigate' (the 'if' for 'of' is the page's). This project builds no plank walks anywhere, so the value is recorded rather than built: it is a negative finding about the ground around the building and never was a build instruction. It belongs in the record because the scene's ground treatment at this corner should be mud, not boards, and because the phrase 'a mere shell' is the closest thing to a description of the fabric that survives.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 4.5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

function.note:
IT CHANGED TRADE ONCE BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND THE SOURCES SAY SO. Andreas: 'It was kept as a saloon and boarding-house by him [Alanson Sweet] and a man from Canada, named Darwin. Then the Couch brothers purchased the property and Ira Couch opened it as a hotel.' Chicago Illustrated (1866), on chicagology_prefire021, calls it 'the first house making any pretensions to the character of a hotel'. Both readings are hotel-keeping in the broad sense and the change is one of style rather than of use; hotel is the value for the scene date because Couch had opened it as one by 1834. It was also a stage stop: the 1874 letter has stages driving to this corner and passengers walking two blocks when the mud beat the horses.

THE TRUSTEES SAT IN THIS HOUSE TWICE IN THE AUTUMN OF 1834 (T-1591). chicago_democrat_1834_10_01#c004 prints an ordinance passed 'At a Meeting of the President and Trustees of the town of Chicago, held at the [Tremon]t House, Sept. [29], 183[4]', and chicago_democrat_1834_10_29#c001 another passed at a meeting 'held at the Tre[mont House in said] town, on the 13th day of [October] A. D. 1834'. Two named sittings of the town's government in this building, four weeks apart and nine months before the scene date: a documented use, which is what is asserted. THE MEETING PLACE IS PARTLY SUPPLIED IN BOTH, and from each other — the first column keeps 'ot House' and the second 'the Tre.' — which is a second printing in the same paper and not a guess; each claim's own note carries the reasoning. WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED IS THE ORDINANCES' CONTENT: one forbids taking earth or sand off a street without the leave of the supervisor of roads, the other empowers the fire wardens to command any bystander at a fire into the line. Both are town law and neither places anything. Nothing on this record's position, form or occupants is changed.

built.note: Andreas: 'In 1833, the first Tremont House ... was built by Alanson Sweet.'

occupants.note: Two sources put Couch here across the scene date and neither leaves a gap. chicagology_prefire021's 1874 letter: 'In 1833 there was built ... the Tremont House, and the following year Ira Couch became its proprietor' - i.e. 1834. Andreas: 'Ira Couch opened it as a hotel. He ran it until 1836, when his brother James took control.' So 1835-07-01 falls squarely inside Ira Couch's tenure. Gale 1902 p 51 now independently names Starr Foot as first proprietor. This corrects the earlier claim that no source held here supported that name; it does not establish a precise tenure or displace Couch on the 1835 scene date. The separate Mallory & Able 1835 claim remains unsupported by the sources held here.

Neither source proves a dated enlargement, and the original picture-match ticket remains open for this substantive source disagreement.

SUPERSEDED TEXT-ONLY STOREY INTERPRETATION:
THE GUARD ON THIS RECORD IS ITS STOREY COUNT, and it is a clean example of how a modern compilation manufactures a fact. chicagology_prefire021 prints, with no typographic break between them, an uncredited editorial summary, a passage of Chicago Illustrated (January 1866) and a reader's letter to the Chicago Tribune of 2 February 1874. The two period texts describe 'a wooden structure' and 'an unpretending frame structure' and count no storeys. The uncredited sentence says 'a three-story wooden building', and that sentence - one modern editor, no source - is where every three-storey Tremont of 1833 comes from, including Wikipedia's and including this project's own dossier, which cites 'chicagology and Wikipedia' as though they were two witnesses. Andreas, the fullest account, gives the building a builder, a corner, a material, four proprietors and a death date, and no height. The record therefore carries two storeys, tagged conjectural, with the three-storey reading argued against on the record rather than dropped. THE SAME PAGE'S HEADER IS WORSE AND MUST NOT BE READ: it gives 'SE corner of Lake and Dearborn Streets' and 'Architect: John M. Van Osdel', both of which belong to the LATER Tremonts, and it contradicts all three body texts on the corner. Andreas independently confirms the move, since the house begun in December 1839 stood 'on the corner where the present Tremont stands'. WHAT IS SOLIDLY ATTESTED, and it is not much: the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn (three times), frame construction (three times), built 1833 by Alanson Sweet, Ira Couch proprietor from 1834, burned 27 October 1839 with seventeen other buildings, and Couch's own description of what he took over - 'a mere shell, without any sidewalk around it, and poorly furnished, as none of the rooms were entirely carpeted, little pieces in front of the bed being considered sufficient for anyone; and very many of the beds were minus one pleasant luxury, a pillow.' A USEFUL SCENE-LEVEL CHECK ON THIS PARCEL: the Chicago American of 15 August 1835, quoted by Andreas, counts the town's stock six weeks after the scene date - 'There are now upward of fifty business houses, four large forwarding-houses, EIGHT TAVERNS, two printing offices, two book-stores, one steam saw-mill, one brewery, one furnace (just going up), and twenty-five mechanics' shops of all kinds.' With this record, the Mansion House and the Exchange Coffee House added, the dataset holds exactly eight public houses for 1835 - Sauganash, Green Tree, Western, Wolf Point, Steamboat, Tremont, Mansion House, Exchange - which is a corroboration of the parcel as a whole rather than of any building in it. See docs/RESEARCH/tremont_house_1.md. THE PLAIN NAME IS CARRIED AS AN AKA (T-0406), because the printed corpus does not use the disambiguator this record is titled with. 'the Tremont House' is what the Chicago Democrat prints - it is the anchor of six advertisements in the gazetteer - and the register resolves an anchor against the committed town by WHOLE-SET equality of identity-bearing words, deliberately, so that 'the store' cannot land on the first store in the town. 'Tremont House (the first)' reduces to {tremont, house, first} and the printed anchor to {tremont, house}, so the two sets were not equal and the register reported that a building this project models, places at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn and draws named nothing the town holds. The '(the first)' in the NAME stays, and stays load-bearing: there was a second Tremont House, begun December 1839 on the corner where the later house stood, and nothing here is a statement that any successor stands in 1835 - the successor is not a committed record at all. The aka is the plain form only, and it still matches whole: 'the Tremont House' resolves here, 'Tremont' alone does not.

OPTIONAL GALE TEXT READING: this two-storey, smaller form is retained for comparison, not asserted as a dated earlier state. The primary reconstruction keeps the actual Gifford picture's three storeys and shutters. Yellow is compatible textual colour evidence in both. No enlargement chronology is invented.
